newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rubin gives Japan time to prove its policies work.
newsitem.headline: Rubin gives Japan time to prove its policies work.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin held off from criticising Japan's economic policies on Friday but served notice that Washington would not wait all that long for Tokyo's financial gamble to work.

Rubin, who stopped here on his way to the Philippines for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers, repeatedly stressed the importance of Japan avoiding a resurgence of its trade surplus by promoting strong demand at home for its products.
"It is essential in our view that Japan's current account surplus not rise significantly," he told reporters at the end of his one-day visit here.
Tokyo is counting on a policy mix of sharp budget cuts coupled with aggressive economic deregulation to keep its economy moving forward and its surplus coming down.

Making clear that he felt that such a stance carried risks, Rubin questioned whether the economic boost from deregulation would be enough to offset the drag on the economy from the fiscal squeeze and this week's rise in Japan's sales tax.
"If the current strategy...doesn't meet the required objectives, then the question will arise what measures will the Japanese government take," he said.
That question could come relatively soon, perhaps before the end of this year, as the economic impact of Japan's fiscal tightening becomes clearer, he suggested.

In that event, Rubin told business leaders, Japan's policy options are "fairly obvious". Although he did not spell them out, Rubin appeared to be thinking of the possibility of Japan introducing a supplementary budget later this year if needed to spur domestic demand and keep down its trade surplus.

Japan's trade surplus in fact has already shown signs of rising, expanding in February for the first time in two years as the weak yen helped make the nation's exports more competitive in world markets.
Rubin warned that a sustained increase in the surplus would run the risk of inciting trade friction with the United States and spurring protectionist pressures worldwide.

"It is critical that Japan's current account surplus not rise again to a level that is detrimental to global growth, that causes trade friction with Japan's trading partners and that could fuel protectionist sentiments," he said.

A rise in the surplus would be particularly unwelcome in the United States, where the Clinton administration already faces troubles ahead in winning a renewal of trade privileges for China and approval of negotiating authority for an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement.

Japan's current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade -- has fallen from the equivalent of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1993 to 1.4 percent. The steep drop in the yen from its 1995 peak has raised the risk of a turnaround, however.
But Rubin rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency -- and thus a weaker U.S. dollar -- was the best way to avoid a renewed rise in the surplus.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," he said.

Rubin reiterated on Friday that a strong dollar has benefits for the United States by keeping down inflation and interest rates. But he added that the U.S. currency has been strong for some time -- an apparent effort to signal that he is not eager to see a further dollar advance.
The dollar rose on Friday, jumping more than one yen to 124 yen in late Asian trade, as the market took Rubin's remarks to mean he would not actively push for a stronger yen.

But it is not clear how long the dollar can stay up if Japan's policy measures fail to keep the trade surplus in check, which would prompt friction with the United States and harsh rhetoric from Washington.
U.S. business leaders have already made clear that they are concerned about the weakness of the yen, which has fallen some 50 percent against the dollar over the past two years.
"At current exchange rates, our profitability here is being killed," Robert Orr, director of government relations for Nippon Motorola Ltd, told Rubin.
